title: Invariant Bilinear Forms
---

A bilinear form $B : V \times V \to \CC$ on a representation $V$ is ***$G$-invariant*** if $B(gv, gw) = B(v, w)$ for all $g \in G$ and $v, w \in V$. Recall from Chapter 9 that a linear map $\varphi : V \to V^*$ determines the bilinear form $B(v, w) = \varphi(v)(w)$, that every bilinear form arises in this way from exactly one $\varphi$, and that $B$ is nondegenerate if and only if $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

:::lemma{16.4.1} Invariant forms and equivariant maps
Let $V^*$ carry the dual representation, $(g\ell)(w) = \ell(g^{-1}w)$. The bilinear form $B$ determined by $\varphi : V \to V^*$ is $G$-invariant if and only if $\varphi$ is $G$-equivariant. So the $G$-invariant bilinear forms on $V$ correspond to the elements of $\Hom_G(V, V^*)$.
:::

:::proof
For $g \in G$ and $v, w \in V$, we have $\varphi(gv)(w) = B(gv, w)$ and $(g\varphi(v))(w) = \varphi(v)(g^{-1}w) = B(v, g^{-1}w)$. So $\varphi$ is equivariant if and only if $B(gv, w) = B(v, g^{-1}w)$ for all $g, v, w$; substituting $w = gw'$, this says $B(gv, gw') = B(v, w')$ for all $g, v, w'$.
:::

:::proposition{16.4.2} Invariant forms on an irreducible representation
Let $V$ be an irreducible representation of $G$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $V \cong V^*$ if and only if $\chi_V$ is real-valued.
2. If $\chi_V$ is not real-valued, the only $G$-invariant bilinear form on $V$ is $0$.
3. If $\chi_V$ is real-valued, $V$ has a nonzero $G$-invariant bilinear form $B$, unique up to a scalar factor. Every nonzero $G$-invariant bilinear form on $V$ is nondegenerate, and $B$ is either symmetric ($B(w, v) = B(v, w)$) or skew-symmetric ($B(w, v) = -B(v, w)$).
:::

:::proof
(i) We have $\chi_{V^*} = \ol{\chi_V}$ (Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3)), and two representations are isomorphic if and only if they have the same character (Corollary [13.5.6](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-6)). So $V \cong V^*$ if and only if $\chi_V = \ol{\chi_V}$.

(ii) and (iii) The dual $V^*$ is irreducible, since $\langle \chi_{V^*}, \chi_{V^*} \rangle = \langle \ol{\chi_V}, \ol{\chi_V} \rangle = \langle \chi_V, \chi_V \rangle = 1$. By Lemma [16.4.1](/notes/math-55a/16-4-invariant-bilinear-forms#lemma-16-4-1), invariant forms correspond to elements of $\Hom_G(V, V^*)$. By Schur’s lemma this space is $0$ if $V \not\cong V^*$. If $\psi : V \to V^*$ is an isomorphism of representations, then every $\varphi \in \Hom_G(V, V^*)$ satisfies $\psi^{-1}\varphi \in \Hom_G(V, V) = \CC \cdot \id$, so $\Hom_G(V, V^*) = \CC \psi$ is 1-dimensional. A nonzero $\varphi$ is an isomorphism by Schur’s lemma, so every nonzero invariant form is nondegenerate. (Directly: $\{v : B(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$ is a subrepresentation, since $B(gv, w) = B(v, g^{-1}w)$, and it is not all of $V$ when $B \neq 0$, so it is $0$.)

Finally, write $B = B^+ + B^-$ with $$B^\pm(v, w) = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(B(v, w) \pm B(w, v)\bigr).$$ Both $B^+$ (symmetric) and $B^-$ (skew-symmetric) are $G$-invariant bilinear forms, so $B^+ = aB$ and $B^- = bB$ for some $a, b \in \CC$ with $a + b = 1$. If $a$ and $b$ were both nonzero, then $B = a^{-1}B^+$ would be symmetric and $B = b^{-1}B^-$ skew-symmetric, so $B(v, w) = B(w, v) = -B(v, w)$ and $B = 0$, a contradiction. Hence $B = B^+$ or $B = B^-$.
:::

:::proposition{16.4.3} Real if and only if symmetric
An irreducible complex representation $V$ of $G$ is real if and only if $V$ carries a nondegenerate $G$-invariant symmetric bilinear form $B : V \times V \to \CC$.
:::

:::proof
($\Rightarrow$) Let $V = (V_0)_{\CC}$. By averaging, $V_0$ has a $G$-invariant inner product $B_0$. Extend it $\CC$-bilinearly: $$B(v_1 + iw_1,\, v_2 + iw_2) = B_0(v_1, v_2) - B_0(w_1, w_2) + i\bigl(B_0(w_1, v_2) + B_0(v_1, w_2)\bigr).$$ This is a symmetric, $G$-invariant, $\CC$-bilinear form on $V$. It is nondegenerate: if $B(v + iw, u) = 0$ for all $u \in V_0$, then $B_0(v, u) + iB_0(w, u) = 0$, so $B_0(v, u) = B_0(w, u) = 0$ for all $u \in V_0$, and $v = w = 0$.

($\Leftarrow$) Choose a $G$-invariant Hermitian inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ on $V$ (Lemma [13.2.1](/notes/math-55a/13-2-maschkes-theorem-and-complete-reducibility#lemma-13-2-1)), conjugate-linear in the first variable. The map $v \mapsto \langle v, \cdot \rangle$ from $V$ to $V^*$ is antilinear and injective, hence bijective, and it is $G$-equivariant: $\langle gv, w \rangle = \langle v, g^{-1}w \rangle$. The form $B$ gives a $G$-equivariant linear isomorphism $\varphi : V \to V^*$, $\varphi(v) = B(v, \cdot)$. Composing $\varphi$ with the inverse of $v \mapsto \langle v, \cdot \rangle$ gives a $G$-equivariant antilinear bijection $\tau : V \to V$, characterized by $$\langle \tau(v), w \rangle = B(v, w) \qquad \text{for all } v, w \in V.$$ The map $\tau^2$ is $\CC$-linear and $G$-equivariant, so by Schur’s lemma $\tau^2 = \lambda \cdot \id$ for some $\lambda \in \CC$. For $v \neq 0$, $$\ol{\lambda}\,\langle v, v \rangle = \langle \tau^2(v), v \rangle = B(\tau(v), v) = B(v, \tau(v)) = \langle \tau(v), \tau(v) \rangle > 0,$$ using the symmetry of $B$ in the third equality and $\tau(v) \neq 0$ (as $\tau$ is bijective) at the end. So $\lambda$ is real and positive. The map $\lambda^{-1/2}\tau$ is still antilinear and $G$-equivariant, and $(\lambda^{-1/2}\tau)^2 = \lambda^{-1}\tau^2 = \id$ because $\lambda^{-1/2}$ is real. By Proposition [16.3.1](/notes/math-55a/16-3-characterizing-real-representations#proposition-16-3-1), $V$ is real.
:::
